title.text: Distributions and sampling: the Gaussian, the central limit theorem, A/B tests and drawing the next word

objects.text: Why can the same question get a different answer from a chat model, and how do we test whether a new AI feature is better?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 14 of 18  |  Probability and statistics
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 14. Last time we learned the vocabulary of probability. Today we meet the shapes that data and models follow, and the tools to reason from a sample. We end with a question you have probably asked yourself: why does a chat model answer the same question differently each time?

By the end of the session you can answer it with arithmetic.

slides.notes:
Three things to take away today. First, describe the Bernoulli, binomial and Gaussian distributions, and work out a binomial probability with factorials. Second, explain the law of large numbers, the central limit theorem, the standard error and a 95 percent confidence interval, and run an A/B test. Third, draw the next word from a probability list with a random number.

That third skill answers why a chat model can give different answers to the same question.

title.text:
Your two hours: distributions,
averages, a test, then drawing a word

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Pictures and hand calculations first. Then the lab on averages, an A/B test and drawing words.

slides.notes:
The first ten minutes recall Session 13 and introduce the question about different answers. Then thirty-five minutes of concepts, with a picture first and a hand example after it. After the break you have forty-five minutes in the lab, in Python or in a spreadsheet, on the same numbers.

We finish with where this appears in AI, an exit check and saving your work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Two fair dice are independent. What does that mean, and what is P(both show 6)?
2.  What is the expectation of a fair die, and what does it mean?
3.  For six learners' scores, do we divide the variance by n or by n - 1, and why?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 13. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Two fair dice are independent. What does that mean, and what is P(both show 6)? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Knowing one die does not change the probabilities of the other. P = 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36.

Question two. What is the expectation of a fair die, and what does it mean? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. 3.5. It is the probability-weighted average over many rolls. No single roll shows it.

Question three. For six learners' scores, do we divide the variance by n or by n - 1, and why? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. By n - 1, because the six are a sample (VAR.S, ddof=1). Dividing by n treats the list as the whole population.

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 13

rows.text: Two fair dice are independent. What does that mean, and what is P(both show 6)?
Knowing one die does not change the probabilities of the other. P = 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36.
What is the expectation of a fair die, and what does it mean?
3.5. It is the probability-weighted average over many rolls. No single roll shows it.
For six learners' scores, do we divide the variance by n or by n - 1, and why?
By n - 1, because the six are a sample (VAR.S, ddof=1). Dividing by n treats the list as the whole population.

objects.text: If an answer surprised you, look back at Session 13 before the lab.

slides.notes:
Three short answers. Two dice are independent: knowing one does not change the probabilities of the other, so the probability that both show six is one sixth times one sixth, one thirty-sixth. Today leans on that idea many times. The expectation of a fair die is 3.5, the weighted average over many rolls, which no single roll shows.

And six learners are a sample, so their variance divides by n minus one, as VAR.S and ddof equals one do. Dividing by n would treat the six as the whole population. Check your own answers against these.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Binomial distribution. The number of successes in n independent yes or no trials, each with probability p.

Gaussian (normal) distribution. The bell curve, set by its mean mu and standard deviation sigma.

Central limit theorem. Averages of many independent values are close to Gaussian, whatever the original shape.

Standard error, confidence interval, p-value. How much a sample mean wanders, a range built from it, and how surprising a gap would be if nothing changed.

Sampling. Drawing a value at random according to its probabilities, as a chat model draws its next word.

title.text:
A Bernoulli trial is one yes or no, and a binomial
counts the yeses in n independent trials

objects.alt: A Bernoulli trial is one yes or no, and a binomial counts the yeses in n independent trials

objects.text: Illustrative: a user rates an answer helpful with p = 0.3. X counts the helpful ratings of 10 users.

runs.text: One user: Bernoulli(p). Mean p, variance p(1 - p) = 0.21.
Independent (Session 13): one rating does not change another.

slides.notes:
The simplest random variable has two outcomes, yes or no. It is called a Bernoulli random variable: one with probability p, zero with probability one minus p. In our illustrative example a user rates a chat answer as helpful with probability 0.3, so the mean is 0.3 and the variance is 0.3 times 0.7, which is 0.21.

Now ask ten users, independently, in the sense of Session 13: one rating does not change another. Count the helpful ratings. That count is a binomial random variable, and the bars show how likely each count is. Three is most likely, because the mean is n times p. The gold bar is exactly three: 0.2668.

title.text:
The binomial formula counts the ways with
factorials, then multiplies the probabilities

objects.alt: The binomial formula counts the ways with factorials, then multiplies the probabilities

rows.text: Multiply every whole number from n down to 1. 0! = 1.
The number of ways to place k successes among n trials: n! / (k! (n - k)!).
p to the k, (1-p) to the n-k
The k trials all succeed, and the other n - k all fail.

objects.text: Spreadsheet: COMBIN(10, 3) = 120. BINOM.DIST(3, 10, 0.3, FALSE) gives the whole answer. TRUE gives P(X at most 3).

slides.notes:
The formula has three parts. The first counts the ways to choose which k of the n trials succeed, and it uses the factorial: n factorial, written n with an exclamation mark, multiplies every whole number from n down to one. Three factorial is six. Ten choose three is ten factorial over three factorial times seven factorial.

Most of the factors cancel, leaving ten times nine times eight over three times two times one, which is 720 over 6, or 120 ways. The second part is the chance that those three succeed, 0.3 cubed. The third is the chance that the other seven fail, 0.7 to the power seven.

Multiply them all and you get 0.2668. Multiplying is allowed because the trials are independent.

title.text:
The Gaussian (normal) distribution is the bell curve,
and 95% of it lies within 1.96 standard deviations

objects.alt: The Gaussian (normal) distribution is the bell curve, and 95% of it lies within 1.96 standard deviations

objects.text: Gaussian (normal): a symmetric bell, centred on the mean mu, width set by sigma.

runs.text: About 68% lies within 1 sigma of mu.
95% lies within 1.96 sigma. Every 95% interval today uses this 1.96.
Averages of many small effects look Gaussian.

slides.notes:
This is the most important shape in statistics, the Gaussian, also called the normal distribution. It is a symmetric bell, centred on the mean mu, and its width is the standard deviation sigma. The horizontal axis counts distance from the mean in standard deviations. About 68 percent of values lie within one sigma of the mean, the dark gold area.

Go out to 1.96 sigma on each side and the area is exactly 95 percent. People often round 1.96 to two. Hold on to 1.96: every 95 percent interval later today is the estimate plus or minus 1.96 of its standard deviations.

title.text:
The Gaussian density, the z-score
and the area to the left of z

objects.alt: The Gaussian density, the z-score and the area to the left of z

rows.text: Quiz scores (illustrative): Normal with mean 60 and standard deviation 10.
How many standard deviations x lies above the mean.
The area to the left of z. erf is a built-in function that computes it.

objects.text: Areas: between z = -1 and 1, 0.6827; between -1.96 and 1.96, 0.9500. Sheet: NORM.DIST(75, 60, 10, TRUE) = 0.9332.

slides.notes:
Three formulas. The density has the mean and the standard deviation in it, but the shape is always the same bell. The z-score tells us how many standard deviations a value is above the mean. Take illustrative quiz scores with mean 60 and standard deviation 10. A score of 75 has z equal to 1.5.

The area to its left is written capital Phi of z, and it is 0.9332, so about 93 percent of learners score below 75. Python computes Phi with a built-in function called erf, as the third line shows, and a spreadsheet uses NORM.DIST. The area between minus 1.96 and 1.96 is 0.95, which is where 1.96 comes from.

title.text:
Recall: two columns at once form a tilted Gaussian
cloud, described by the covariance matrix

objects.alt: Recall: two columns at once form a tilted Gaussian cloud, described by the covariance matrix

objects.text: Means (4, 6). Sample covariance matrix (Session 13): variances 5.6 and 8.4, covariance 5.

runs.text: Ellipses: 1 and 2 sd. Red arrows: eigenvectors (PCA, Session 6).
Eigenvalues 12.19 and 1.81: the variance along each arrow.
130 of 150 simulated points: scores outside 0 to 10 are left out.

slides.notes:
A recall slide, joining Sessions 5, 6 and 13. With two columns, study hours and score, the Gaussian becomes a cloud. Its centre is the vector of means, four and six. Its shape is an ellipse, tilted by the covariance. The numbers are the sample covariance matrix of our six learners from last session: variances 5.6 and 8.4 on the diagonal, covariance 5 off it.

The red arrows are its eigenvectors, the principal components of Session 6, and the eigenvalues 12.19 and 1.81 are the variances along them. A real score cannot leave the range zero to ten, so simulated points outside it are not drawn.

title.text:
The law of large numbers: the more repeats,
the closer the average gets to the true mean

objects.alt: The law of large numbers: the more repeats, the closer the average gets to the true mean

objects.text: Two runs of rolling a die 10,000 times (simulation). The line is the running average.

runs.text: After 1 roll the average is one of 1 to 6, often far from 3.5.
After 100 rolls it is near 3.5.
After 10,000 rolls it is usually within about 0.03 of 3.5.

slides.notes:
The law of large numbers says that the more independent repeats you average, the closer the average gets to the true mean. These are two simulated runs of rolling a die ten thousand times. The horizontal axis is logarithmic, so the early rolls get room. After a single roll the average is that one roll, any of one to six, so it is often far off.

In these two runs it started at one and at six. By a hundred rolls both lines are near 3.5, and by ten thousand they are very close. Our sixty fixed rolls from Session 13 had a mean of 3.97. Sixty is too few to settle.

title.text:
The central limit theorem: averages of many
rolls look Gaussian, though a single die is flat

objects.alt: The central limit theorem: averages of many rolls look Gaussian, though a single die is flat

objects.text: Each panel: 20,000 averages of n dice. n = 1 is flat, not Gaussian. At n = 30 the red curve fits.

slides.notes:
The central limit theorem as a picture. Each panel shows twenty thousand averages. On the left, the average of one die is a single die, flat, with six bars. The average of two dice is a triangle. With five dice the shape is already a bell. With thirty dice it is almost exactly the red Gaussian curve, and it is also much narrower.

The theorem says this happens for averages of independent values from almost any starting shape, as long as there are enough of them. That explains why the Gaussian appears everywhere. Why is the last panel so much narrower?

title.text:
Standard error: how much
a sample mean wanders

objects.alt: Standard error: how much a sample mean wanders

rows.text: The mean of a sample of n independent values.
Standard deviation of one value, and the sample size. The die's sigma is known (Session 13), so no n - 1 here.
Standard error: the standard deviation of the sample mean.

objects.text: Four times the data halves the SE. Simulated 30-dice averages (seed 14): standard deviation 0.311.

slides.notes:
The picture in formulas. The mean of n independent values is close to Gaussian, centred on the true mean mu, with standard deviation sigma over the square root of n. That standard deviation of the sample mean is called the standard error. For a die we know sigma exactly from its probabilities, 1.7078, so nothing is estimated and no n minus one appears.

For thirty dice, 1.7078 divided by the square root of thirty is 0.3118, and the simulation gave 0.311. To halve the standard error you need four times the data.

title.text:
A 95% confidence interval comes from a method that
catches the true mean in about 95 of 100 samples

objects.alt: A 95% confidence interval comes from a method that catches the true mean in about 95 of 100 samples

objects.text: 20 samples of 30 dice (simulation). 19 of the 20 intervals contain the true mean 3.5. The red one misses.

runs.text: Interval = sample mean plus or minus 1.96 standard errors: the 95% band of the Gaussian.
The 95% describes the method over many samples.
It is not the chance that this one interval holds the true value.

slides.notes:
A confidence interval gives a range for the true mean instead of a single guess. For each sample of thirty dice we compute the mean, then go 1.96 standard errors to each side. Why 1.96?

The sample mean is close to Gaussian, and 95 percent of a Gaussian lies within 1.96 standard deviations. Twenty samples are shown. 19 of the twenty intervals catch the true mean, 3.5, and the red one misses. That matches the promise: about 95 out of 100 intervals catch it.

Be careful with the wording. The 95 percent describes the method over many samples. Once an interval is computed, the true mean is either inside or outside it.

title.text:
Confidence interval for a mean,
worked on the 60 fixed rolls

objects.alt: Confidence interval for a mean, worked on the 60 fixed rolls

rows.text: The mean of the 60 rolls from Session 13, and the sample size.
Sample standard deviation: sigma is unknown, so estimate it with n - 1 (STDEV.S).
Standard error s over the square root of n.
Phi(1.96) = 0.975, so 95% of a Gaussian lies between -1.96 and 1.96.

objects.text: With only 60 rolls a statistician uses the t value 2.00: 3.506 to 4.428, and 3.5 is still just outside.

slides.notes:
An interval by hand. Our sixty fixed rolls had a mean of 3.9667. In real work sigma is unknown, so we estimate it from the sample, and an estimate from a sample divides by n minus one, as in Session 13. That gives s equal to 1.7847. The standard error is s divided by the square root of sixty, 0.2304.

The interval is the mean plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, from 3.515 to 4.418. 3.5 is just outside. We know the true mean is 3.5, so this sample is one of the roughly one in twenty that misses. With so few rolls a statistician would use the t value, 2.00, in place of 1.96, and 3.5 is still just outside.

title.text:
An A/B test splits users at random into
two groups and compares one rate

objects.alt: An A/B test splits users at random into two groups and compares one rate

objects.text: Illustrative counts: a new suggested follow-up feature in an AI chat app. Metric: share of chats rated helpful.

runs.text: Random assignment makes the groups alike, apart from the feature.
B beats A by 2.0 percentage points.
Question: a real effect, or luck?

slides.notes:
A decision you may face. A team adds a new feature to an AI chat app, suggested follow-up questions, and wants to know if it helps. They split users at random into group A with the current app and group B with the new feature, then count chats rated helpful.

These counts are illustrative. A had 288 of 2,400, which is 12.0%. B had 336 of 2,400, which is 14.0%. The gap is 2.0 percentage points. Is that a real effect, or could it be luck? A hypothesis test answers that.

title.text:
A hypothesis test asks how likely a gap this
large would be if the feature did nothing

objects.alt: A hypothesis test asks how likely a gap this large would be if the feature did nothing

objects.text: Null hypothesis: the true rates are equal. Our gap is z = 2.06 standard errors.

runs.text: The gold tails hold gaps at least this large, in either direction. Their area is the p-value: 0.039.
A common, arbitrary convention calls p < 0.05 "significant".
Small p-value: this gap would be rare by luck alone.

slides.notes:
A hypothesis test starts from a sceptical assumption, the null hypothesis, which says the two true rates are equal. If that were true, the gap between the groups would still wobble by chance, following this bell curve, measured in standard errors. Our actual gap sits at z equal to 2.06.

The gold tails show the probability of a gap at least that large in either direction. That area is the p-value, 0.039. Many fields use a threshold of 0.05 and call smaller p-values significant. The threshold is a convention with nothing special about it, and a small p-value says nothing about how big the effect is.

title.text: The two-proportion z-test

objects.alt: The two-proportion z-test

rows.text: The rate in each group: helpful chats k divided by users n.
The pooled rate: (k_A + k_B) / (n_A + n_B), both groups together.
The standard error of the gap, and the gap in standard errors.

objects.text: Two-sided p-value = 2 × (1 - Phi(z)) = 0.0394. Spreadsheet: 2*(1-NORM.DIST(z,0,1,TRUE)).

slides.notes:
The test itself. If the null hypothesis is true, both groups share one rate, so we pool the counts: 624 helpful chats out of 4,800, which is 0.13. The standard error of the gap uses that pooled rate and both sample sizes, and it comes to 0.00971. The z statistic is the observed gap divided by the standard error, 2.060.

The two-sided p-value is twice the area beyond z, which is 0.0394. The table that follows puts every step in one place.

title.text:
The A/B test step by step,
with a 95% interval for the gap

rows.text: 2 × (1 - area to the left of z)

objects.text: Step 3 pools because the test assumes no difference. Step 6 does not assume that: SE = sqrt(p_A(1-p_A)/n_A + p_B(1-p_B)/n_B). The interval, 0.1 to 3.9 points, only just excludes 0.

slides.notes:
The whole test in one table, with illustrative counts. Step one, the two rates. Step two, the pooled rate, 0.13. Step three, the standard error of the gap. Step four, z equals 2.06. Step five, the p-value, 0.0394. And step six, a 95 percent confidence interval for the gap itself, again plus or minus 1.96 standard errors: from 0.1 to 3.9 percentage points.

The interval only just excludes zero. It tells you more than the p-value alone, because it shows the effect could be tiny. A careful team might run the test longer.

title.text: A p-value is easy to misread

objects.alt: check

objects.text: A p-value is

runs.text: The probability of a gap at least this large, either way, if there were truly no difference

objects.alt: cross

objects.text: A p-value is not

runs.text: The probability that the feature does nothing
The size of the effect

objects.text: Testing many features: of 20 useless ones, about 1 passes the 0.05 line by luck. Report the gap and its interval.

slides.notes:
A warning. A p-value is the probability of seeing a gap at least this large, in either direction, if there were truly no difference. That is all. It is not the probability that the feature does nothing, and it says nothing about how big or how useful the effect is.

A tiny effect can have a tiny p-value with enough users. A separate trap comes from testing many things at once: test twenty useless features and about one will pass the 0.05 line by luck alone. So always report the gap and its interval next to the p-value.

title.text:
Sampling from a distribution: cut 0 to 1 into
slices and see where a random number lands

objects.alt: Sampling from a distribution: cut 0 to 1 into slices and see where a random number lands

objects.text: The next-word list of Session 13. Each word owns a slice as wide as its probability. Draw a random number u between 0 and 1.

runs.text: u = 0.62 lands in the coffee slice (0.446 to 0.745).
Draw again and u differs, so the word can differ.
Likely words are picked often, unlikely ones sometimes.

slides.notes:
How does a program pick a word from a probability list?

It cuts the line from zero to one into slices, one per word, as wide as each probability. Tea owns the first 0.446, coffee the next 0.299, and so on. The slice edges are running totals. Then it draws a random number between zero and one. Here u is 0.62, which falls in the coffee slice, between 0.446 and 0.745, so the program outputs coffee.

Draw again, and u will be different, so the word can be different. That answers the first half of today's question. Session 17 adds the settings that reshape the slices first. The numbers are illustrative.

title.text:
Bridge: sample the central limit theorem
and the next word with NumPy

runs.text: rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
means = rng.integers(1, 7, (20000, 30)).mean(axis=1)
means.mean(), means.std(ddof=1)
np.cumsum([1, 2, 3])
# running totals: 1, 3, 6
cum = np.cumsum(p)
# slice edges
np.searchsorted(cum, 0.62)

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 2: 20,000 samples of 30 dice. mean(axis=1) averages each row.
Line 3: the mean is near 3.5; the standard deviation is near the standard error 0.3118 (0.311 with seed 14).
Line 4: np.cumsum gives running totals.
Lines 6 and 7: the slice edges, then the first edge that reaches u: 1 = coffee.
Spreadsheet: NORM.DIST, BINOM.DIST and fixed sample columns replace the random draws.

slides.notes:
The code you will use. The first block repeats the central limit theorem experiment. Generate twenty thousand rows of thirty dice, average each row, and look at the mean and standard deviation of those averages, with ddof equal to one because they are a sample of averages. np.cumsum adds as it goes, giving running totals.

You need it twice in the lab: for the running average of the law of large numbers, and for the slice edges. np.searchsorted then finds the first edge that reaches u, which is the drawn word. In the spreadsheet we use fixed columns, so the numbers do not move.

Errors you will meet, what
they mean and what to do

rows.text: Your sample numbers differ from the slides
Use Run all from the top. Every random step makes its own seeded generator.
You used one tail. Double the tail area for a two-sided test.
The last argument was TRUE. Use FALSE for exactly 3.
You divided by n. The sample s uses n - 1: STDEV.S or ddof=1.
A draw picks the word one slice too late
u belongs to the first slice whose running total reaches u.

slides.notes:
The errors you will probably meet. If your simulated numbers differ from the slides, check that the seeded generator line ran first. A p-value of 0.0197 means you used one tail instead of two. In the spreadsheet, BINOM.DIST with TRUE gives the probability of at most three, which differs from exactly three.

An interval that is a little too narrow usually means the standard deviation divided by n, so use STDEV.S or ddof equal to one. And a draw that lands one word late has skipped the slice whose running total first reaches u.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: a language model draws
its next token at random from its probabilities

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: a language model draws its next token at random from its probabilities

objects.text: Published language models produce a probability for every token, and sampling draws one of them.

runs.text: A new random number each time: the same question can get a different answer.
Public APIs document settings that reshape the list first: temperature and top-p (Session 17).

slides.notes:
Today in real systems. A published language model of this kind ends with a probability for every token in its vocabulary, as you saw in Session 13. When it samples, it draws a random number and takes the token whose slice it lands in, exactly as you did by hand.

Each answer uses new random numbers, which is why the same question can come back differently. The public APIs of OpenAI, Google Gemini and Anthropic document settings, temperature and top-p, that reshape the list before the draw. Session 17 teaches both. What a product does beyond these documented settings is not public.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: an A/B test shows
whether a new AI feature really is better

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: an A/B test shows whether a new AI feature really is better

objects.text: Online experiments compare two versions of a product on one measured rate.

runs.text: Published practice: Kohavi, Tang and Xu describe it in their 2020 book on online controlled experiments.
The mathematics is the same as today. Which AI features a company tests is its own business.

slides.notes:
The same mathematics in practice. Teams that build products with language models compare versions with online experiments. They split users at random, measure one rate such as helpful ratings, and run the same test you ran today. The method is published, for example in the 2020 book by Kohavi, Tang and Xu on online controlled experiments.

We do not know which features a specific company tests, so I make no claim about that. The decision also weighs the size of the effect and the cost, as well as the p-value.

A short activity. Give any AI assistant our A and B counts and ask for the z statistic, the two-sided p-value and a 95 percent interval for the gap. Compare with our numbers: z of 2.06, p of 0.039, and an interval of 0.1 to 3.9 percentage points.

title.text: Exit check: three questions

rows.text: A fair coin is flipped 10 times. What are the mean and standard deviation of the number of heads?
n p = 5 and the square root of 10 × 0.5 × 0.5, which is 1.581.
A test gives p = 0.03. Does that mean a 3% chance the feature does nothing?
No. It is the chance of a gap this large if there is truly no difference.
With the slices of today, which word does u = 0.90 pick, and why can the next answer differ?
Milk (0.893 to 0.967). The next draw uses a new random number.

slides.notes:
Three questions to finish. First, ten fair coin flips: the mean number of heads is n times p, which is five, and the standard deviation is the square root of 10 times 0.5 times 0.5, about 1.58. Second, a p-value of 0.03 does not mean a three percent chance that the feature does nothing.

It is the chance of a gap this large if there is truly no difference. Third, u equal to 0.90 lands in the milk slice, between 0.893 and 0.967, and the next answer can differ because it draws a new random number. Write your answers in your lab file.
